cards.front: What should you know about permanent magnet?
cards.back: A magnet that produces its own magnetic field all the time. It always has a north pole and a south pole. Examples: bar magnets, fridge magnets, compass needles.

cards.front: What should you know about induced magnet?
cards.back: A material that becomes magnetic when placed in the magnetic field of a permanent magnet. It loses most or all of its magnetism when removed from the field. Induced magnets are always attracted towards the permanent magnet (never repelled).

cards.front: What should you know about magnetic field?
cards.back: The region around a magnet where a magnetic force can be experienced. The field is strongest near the poles of the magnet.

cards.front: What should you know about magnetic field lines?
cards.back: Lines that show the direction and strength of a magnetic field. They always go from north to south (outside the magnet). The closer the lines, the stronger the field.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Magnets And Magnetic Fields
cards.back: Not all metals are magnetic. Copper, aluminium, gold and silver are NOT magnetic. Never assume a material is magnetic just because it is a metal.

cards.front: What should you know about rules for magnetic poles?
cards.back: • Like poles repel (N–N or S–S) • Unlike poles attract (N–S) • A magnet always has two poles — it is impossible to have a single pole (a monopole). If you cut a magnet in half, you get two smaller magnets, each with N and S poles.

cards.front: What should you know about using iron filings?
cards.back: Sprinkle iron filings around a magnet on a flat surface. The filings align along the field lines, showing the shape of the magnetic field. This is quick but not precise.

cards.front: What should you know about using a compass?
cards.back: Place a small plotting compass near the magnet. The compass needle points along the field line. Mark the position of each end of the needle. Move the compass so the tail of the needle is at the marked head position. Repeat to plot the complete field line. This method shows the direction of the field.

cards.front: What should you know about earth's magnetic field?
cards.back: The Earth's core acts like a giant magnet, creating a magnetic field that extends into space. The geographic North Pole is actually near the magnetic south pole (because the north pole of a compass points towards it — it attracts the north-seeking pole). Compasses align with Earth's field and point towards magnetic north.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Magnets And Magnetic Fields
cards.back: Interpreting magnetic field diagrams: the closer the field lines, the stronger the field. Field line density is proportional to field strength. When comparing magnets, count the number of field lines per unit area near the poles to compare strengths qualitatively.

cards.front: What should you know about answers?
cards.back: (a) Iron, steel and cobalt were attracted. They are all magnetic materials. (b) The statement is incorrect — copper and aluminium ARE metals, but they are non-magnetic metals. Being a metal does not mean a material is magnetic. Only iron, nickel, cobalt and steel are magnetic. (c) The iron nail will also stick to the south pole. Iron is an induced magnet — it becomes magnetised when placed in any external magnetic field and is always attracted to the permanent magnet regardless of which pole is used. Unlike permanent magnets, induced magnets cannot be repelled.

cards.front: What does Produces own magnetic field? mean?
cards.back: Yes — always magnetic (e.g. No — only magnetic in another magnet's field)

cards.front: What does Can be switched off? mean?
cards.back: No (e.g. Yes — loses magnetism when removed from field)

cards.front: What does Attracted or repelled by permanent magnet? mean?
cards.back: Attracted OR repelled (depending on pole) (e.g. Only attracted (never repelled))
Bar magnet, compass needle, fridge magnet (e.g. Iron nail near a bar magnet, paper clip attracted to magnet)
